abstract: AI structure predictors accept post-translationally modified (PTM) residues, but whether they place the added atoms where crystallography finds them, and whether their confidence reveals when they do not, is unknown. We first built a ruler from experiment alone: independent crystal structures of the same site reproduce the added atoms of oxidised cysteine and methionine to 0.32 [A], the closest pre-cutoff library rotamer lies at 0.41 [A] and a model-free guess at 4.17 [A]. We then predicted 176 hold-out PTM sites, released after every model's training cut-off, with RareFold, Boltz-2, Chai-1 and AlphaFold 3, using identical inputs and thresholds fixed before measurement. On oxidised Cys/Met (up to 34 sites in 25 proteins), the three all-atom models place the matching distal atoms of neighbouring canonical side chains to 0.35-0.38 [A] but the added oxygens at 1.19-1.51 [A]; 29-41 % of placements are wrong by more than 2 [A], as sterically plausible rotamers that the electron density does not support. RareFold misplaces ordinary side chains as well. Across all PTM classes, residue confidence does not flag the failure: at pLDDT [≥] 90, 24-46 % of modified-residue placements are catastrophic, 3.5-5 times the rate for matched canonical atoms. One seed rarely samples the correct rotamer; more seeds sample it more often, yet the models' own ranking does not select it. Methyllysine shows the same gap, whereas for pyridoxal-lysine the models diverge (AlphaFold 3 1.13 [A], Boltz-2 4.96 [A]). A high residue pLDDT at a modified residue therefore does not verify its side chain.
